sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Can a socially optimal outcome be destabilized by a coalition whose members all gain? The Max- k k -Cut game provides a natural setting for this question. Players are vertices of a graph, each chooses one of k k colors, and each benefits from neighbors choosing different colors. Consider, for example, transmitters selecting among k k communication channels. An edge joins two transmitters that interfere when assigned the same channel. In a simple unweighted model, each transmitter seeks to minimize the number of interfering neighbors on its channel, equivalently maximizing the number assigned different channels. A channel assignment is therefore a coloring , and the utility of each transmitter is the number of its neighbors assigned a different channel. An edge whose endpoints have different colors is called bichromatic and represents a pair of transmitters whose interference is avoided. Since each such edge contributes one unit to the utilities of both endpoints, maximizing total utility, or social welfare , is equivalent to finding a maximum k k -cut or equivalently, an optimal coloring: a coloring with the largest possible number of bichromatic edges. At an optimal coloring, no transmitter can benefit by changing its channel alone, since such an improvement would also increase the number of bichromatic edges, contradicting optimality. Thus every optimal coloring is also a Nash equilibrium , an outcome in which no player can gain by changing its choice alone. Transmitters may, however, coordinate their channel changes, potentially benefiting every participant at the expense of those outside the coordinating group. Stability against such coordinated changes is more demanding: a strong Nash equilibrium , or simply strong equilibrium , is an outcome in which no group of players, called a coalition , can change their choices jointly so that every member strictly gains, while the choices of players outside the coalition remain fixed ( Aumann, 1959 ) . Whether every optimal coloring is a strong equilibrium has been a central open problem in the study of unweighted Max- k k -Cut games ( Carosi et al., 2019 ; Garuglieri et al., 2024 ) . We answer this question negatively for every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , even on connected graphs. The counterexample preserves the cut value: coalition members gain by eliminating internal conflicts, while players outside the coalition bear the corresponding losses. For every integer k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , there exists a finite simple, connected, unweighted graph that admits an optimal k k -coloring which is not a strong equilibrium. In our example, the coalition deviates to another optimal coloring: every member strictly gains, although total social welfare remains unchanged. Section 2 presents the construction and establishes its optimality through a combinatorial count, completing the proof of Theorem 2 . Motivated by this example, Section 3 examines how changes in conflicts within a coalition enable its members to gain. It derives consequences for deviations from optimal colorings and bounds the internal conflicts that can remain after deviations from general Nash equilibria.

sections.heading: 4 Concluding remarks
sections.text: Social optimality guarantees stability against unilateral deviations in Max- k k -Cut games, but our result shows that this guarantee does not extend to coalitions, even on simple, connected, unweighted graphs. For every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , an optimal coloring can admit a joint deviation that strictly benefits every participating player. Moreover, the deviation can preserve social welfare: the coalition’s gains are offset by losses to players outside it. Maximizing aggregate welfare therefore does not, by itself, remove the incentive for coordinated departures from a socially optimal outcome. The internal-conflict analysis can help to identify conditions under which stability is restored. The deviation identity relates the coalition’s gains to the change in cut value and the conflicts removed within the coalition, recovering the known maximum-degree condition for stability of optimal colorings. For deviations from general Nash equilibria, the sharp bound on surviving internal conflicts also shows why coalition size alone cannot control these conflicts: the density of the subgraph induced by the coalition plays an essential role. The counterexample leaves two distinct questions open: does every unweighted Max- k k -Cut game admit a strong equilibrium, and does it always admit an optimal coloring that is a strong equilibrium? Disproving stability of every optimum does not rule out the possibility of selecting a stable optimum. This distinction suggests a natural direction for further work: to determine when social optimality and coalitional stability can be achieved simultaneously, and how such colorings can be found. Characterizing the graph structures that permit this compatibility would help turn welfare maximization into a prescription that also accounts for players’ incentives to coordinate.

A recurring conjecture in the literature asserts that, for unweighted graphs, every optimal coloring has this stability property, known as strong equilibrium. We disprove the conjecture for every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 by exhibiting a finite, simple, connected, unweighted graph with an optimal coloring that is not a strong equilibrium. The profitable coalitional deviation leads to another optimal coloring: every coalition member gains, while players outside the coalition bear the corresponding losses and social welfare remains unchanged. We also give an exact identity relating coalitional gains, changes in cut value, and internal conflicts, recovering the known stability guarantee for optimal colorings when the maximum degree is at most 2 ​ k − 1 2k-1 . For strong deviations from general Nash equilibria, we establish a sharp upper bound on the number of monochromatic edges remaining within the coalition and show that this number can exceed the coalition size. keywords Max- k k -Cut games, Strong equilibria, Coalitional deviations, Optimal colorings, Graph partitioning 1 Introduction Can a socially optimal outcome be destabilized by a coalition whose members all gain? The Max- k k -Cut game provides a natural setting for this question. Players are vertices of a graph, each chooses one of k k colors, and each benefits from neighbors choosing different colors. Consider, for example, transmitters selecting among k k communication channels. An edge joins two transmitters that interfere when assigned the same channel. In a simple unweighted model, each transmitter seeks to minimize the number of interfering neighbors on its channel, equivalently maximizing the number assigned different channels. A channel assignment is therefore a coloring , and the utility of each transmitter is the number of its neighbors assigned a different channel. An edge whose endpoints have different colors is called bichromatic and represents a pair of transmitters whose interference is avoided. Since each such edge contributes one unit to the utilities of both endpoints, maximizing total utility, or social welfare , is equivalent to finding a maximum k k -cut or equivalently, an optimal coloring: a coloring with the largest possible number of bichromatic edges. At an optimal coloring, no transmitter can benefit by changing its channel alone, since such an improvement would also increase the number of bichromatic edges, contradicting optimality. Thus every optimal coloring is also a Nash equilibrium , an outcome in which no player can gain by changing its choice alone. Transmitters may, however, coordinate their channel changes, potentially benefiting every participant at the expense of those outside the coordinating group. Stability against such coordinated changes is more demanding: a strong Nash equilibrium , or simply strong equilibrium , is an outcome in which no group of players, called a coalition , can change their choices jointly so that every member strictly gains, while the choices of players outside the coalition remain fixed ( Aumann, 1959 ) . Whether every optimal coloring is a strong equilibrium has been a central open problem in the study of unweighted Max- k k -Cut games ( Carosi et al., 2019 ; Garuglieri et al., 2024 ) . We answer this question negatively for every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , even on connected graphs. Its mechanism is the elimination of internal conflicts: the coalition removes sixteen monochromatic edges within the core, allowing every member to gain one unit of utility while the cut value remains unchanged. We first formalize this mechanism through an identity relating the coalition’s total gain to the change in its internal conflicts. This yields a necessary condition for a strong deviation from an optimal coloring and a sufficient condition for optimal colorings to be strong equilibria.
